title.en: Responsible Data Practice and Conduct in Analytical Work
title.ar: الممارسة المسؤولة للبيانات وقواعد السلوك في العمل التحليلي

tagline: Handle an analytical request lawfully and fairly: test it against the PDPL, classify and share with conditions, release tables that single nobody out, compare groups honestly, document the work and hold the conversation that rescopes an unsafe request
description: Participants handle an analytical engagement for a fictional university's student-success unit. They test requests against the Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL), classify the data and decide what may be shared with a government partner, suppress small cells in aggregate outputs, compare outcome and error rates across student groups, keep an analysis log and a datasheet, and handle three stakeholder conversations: scoping, pushing back on an unsafe request and explaining limits. Deeper de-identification and fairness audits are in DS-309.
audience: Practitioners. Graduates and early-career analysts who have completed the FN courses or passed the placement test, and analysts moving into data science.
prerequisites: FN-106 Responsible Data and AI Practice in the Kingdom
Computes rates and a confidence interval for a proportion by group in SQL or a dataframe
Has written a short analytical report for a non-specialist reader

outcomes.text: Explain the PDPL principles and the classification and sharing rules an analysis engages, from lawful basis to data subjects' rights and transfer, given five analysis requests from the case
outcomes.evidence: a note per request naming the rules engaged, at least four of five right

outcomes.text: Classify the datasets and outputs of an analysis and decide what may be shared, with whom and in what form, given the student records, a partner's sharing request and the classification policy
outcomes.evidence: a classification and sharing table with the control each decision requires

outcomes.text: Apply aggregation and small-cell suppression to results tables and check that no student can be singled out, given draft tables by college, nationality and disability status
outcomes.evidence: release-ready tables and a log of each suppressed cell and the reason

outcomes.text: Analyse referral and error rates across student groups and report differences with their uncertainty and possible causes, given a support-referral rule and its results by group
outcomes.evidence: rates with intervals and two possible bias types with the check that separates them

outcomes.text: Prepare a datasheet and an analysis log that let a reviewer trace each result to its data, decisions and approvals, given the case analysis and a template
outcomes.evidence: a datasheet and log a peer uses to answer five audit questions

outcomes.text: Lead a stakeholder conversation that rescopes an unsafe or unclear request into a lawful, answerable question, and record the agreement, given a role-played sponsor asking for an individual-level risk list
outcomes.evidence: an observed role-play scored on a rubric and a written scope note

case_study.name: Al-Qimam University, Student Success Unit
case_study.summary: Al-Qimam University is a fictional public university with six colleges. Its Student Success Unit runs Awn, a rule that refers students to academic support from attendance and midterm marks, and its analyst is asked to evaluate the rule, publish tables, answer a government partner and serve three sponsors. All 18,000 student records are synthetic, generated with a fixed seed, and planted with the problems the labs find: identifiers in free-text notes, small cells that a subtraction recovers, attendance that is under-recorded for one group, marks that are missing for another, a gap that vanishes inside colleges, and a sharing request that asks for too much.

format_note: Intensive: 3 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task

days.title: Lawful analysis

sessions.title: What the law asks of an analyst
sessions.summary: Every analysis request engages a small set of PDPL rules, and an analyst who can name them knows when to proceed and when to ask
outcomes: Name the PDPL rules an analysis request engages, from lawful basis to transfer
Distinguish analysis inside the collection purpose from a new purpose, a disclosure and a transfer
Decide which requests go to the data protection officer before any data is touched

lab.title: Five requests, which rules
lab.summary: Map five requests to the PDPL principles they engage, and write the note that says so for one of them.

steps.text: Read the five requests and the privacy notice
Name the kind of processing each request is
Mark the rules each request engages
Flag the requests that go to the data protection officer
Write the note for one request

lab.stretch: Add a sixth request: a student asks for a copy of her data used in the analysis

sessions.title: Purpose, minimisation and secondary use
sessions.summary: The purpose decides the fields: what it does not need is dropped or coarsened, and a new purpose is a new decision
outcomes: Write a purpose precise enough to decide each field against
Cut an extract to the fields the purpose needs, keeping, coarsening or dropping each with a reason
Recognise a secondary use and name what the law and the national rules require before it starts

lab.title: Cut the extract
lab.summary: Cut an extract to the fields the purpose needs, recording why, and find the identifiers hiding in free text.

steps.text: Read the purpose and the 30 columns of the registry
Decide keep, coarsen or drop for each field, with a reason
Scan the advisor notes for identifiers with rules
Build the extract with a project pseudonym
Write the minimisation log

lab.stretch: Decide the fields again for a second purpose, the partner's study, and say what makes it a secondary use

sessions.title: Classifying data and outputs
sessions.summary: Tables, charts and lists are data too: each gets a level from the impact of its disclosure, and the level sets the controls
outcomes: Classify a dataset or an output with the impact questions of the Data Classification Policy
Apply the highest-level rule to combined data and say when an aggregate can be Public
Name the control each level requires, including what may be entered into an AI tool

lab.title: Classify and control
lab.summary: Classify four datasets and three outputs and name each control.

steps.text: Run the impact questions on the four datasets
Classify the three outputs
Apply the highest-level rule to a joined file
Name the controls for each item
Decide what may be entered into an AI tool

lab.stretch: Set a declassification trigger for the referral table and say who approves it

sessions.title: Sharing requests
sessions.summary: A partner's request is judged on purpose, minimum data and the source's consent, then answered with a form of release and conditions
outcomes: Assess a sharing request against the tests of the Data Sharing Policy and the rules for secondary use
Choose the form of release: record level, pseudonymised or aggregate
Draft approval conditions under the policy's control headings and name who signs

lab.title: The Observatory's request
lab.summary: Assess a partner's sharing request and draft the approval conditions.

steps.text: Read the request and name the parties and the route
Assess it against the three tests
Choose the form of release
Draft the conditions under the eight control headings
Fill the decision record and name who signs

lab.stretch: The partner adds a consultant outside the Kingdom: revise the decision

days.subtitle: Test the request, cut the data, classify it and decide what a partner may have

days.title: Fair and safe outputs

sessions.title: Aggregate release and small cells
sessions.summary: An aggregate table can still point at one student: small cells, totals and a second table are the three ways
outcomes: Explain how a small cell, a total or a second release singles out a student
Apply a threshold rule with complementary suppression and log each suppressed cell
Test a release for recovery by subtraction and by differencing before it leaves

lab.title: Suppress, then attack
lab.summary: Apply a threshold rule and test for singling out by differencing.

steps.text: Count the cells under the threshold in three draft tables
Suppress them and log each cell with its reason
Recover a suppressed cell from the totals
Add complementary suppression and test again
Difference the table against an earlier release

lab.stretch: Round the counts to a base of 5 in place of suppression and compare what a reader loses

sessions.title: Where bias enters
sessions.summary: Bias enters before any metric is computed: in what is recorded, who is covered, how the outcome is defined and how the result is used
outcomes: Trace a rule's data from the event to the decision and mark where bias can enter
Distinguish a recording problem, a coverage problem, a label problem and a use problem
Measure one entry point with data instead of arguing about it

lab.title: Four entry points
lab.summary: Mark four points where bias can enter the referral data, and measure two of them.

steps.text: Trace Awn's data from the event to the referral
Mark four points where bias can enter
Measure the attendance record against the roll-call audit
Measure missing midterm marks by group
Rank which entry point to check first

lab.stretch: Find a fifth entry point after the referral: who takes up the support that is offered

sessions.title: Comparing groups
sessions.summary: A fair comparison reports the referral rate and both error rates by group, each with its interval, inside the strata that matter
outcomes: Compute referral, false-referral and missed-student rates by group
Report each rate and each difference with a confidence interval
Check whether a gap survives inside colleges before explaining it

lab.title: Rates with intervals
lab.summary: Compare referral and error rates by group with intervals.

steps.text: Build the four outcome counts by group
Compute the three rates with Wilson intervals
Compute the differences with their intervals
Check the gender gap inside each college
Write the result in one sentence per gap

lab.stretch: Compute the rates for one intersection of two groups and say what the interval allows you to claim

sessions.title: Naming the bias
sessions.summary: A gap has more than one possible cause: name two bias types from the national guide and run the check that separates them
outcomes: Match an observed gap to candidate bias types in the AI Bias Reference Guide
Design the check that separates two candidate causes
State what a fairness metric cannot settle and who decides the rest

lab.title: Two gaps, two names
lab.summary: Match two observed gaps to bias types in the national guide and run the check that separates them.

steps.text: Read the two gaps and their intervals
Pick two candidate bias types for each gap
Design the check that separates them
Run the two checks
Record the conclusion and what stays open

lab.stretch: Change the rule to equalise false referrals and report what happens to missed students

days.subtitle: Release tables that single nobody out, and compare groups with honest uncertainty

days.title: Professional conduct

sessions.title: Datasheets and analysis logs
sessions.summary: A reviewer who was not in the room must be able to trace a number to its data, its decisions and its approvals
outcomes: Fill a datasheet that states what the data is, how it was collected and what it must not be used for
Keep an analysis log in which every decision has a reason, a date and an approver
Tie a release to a version so a result can be traced and rerun

lab.title: Datasheet and log
lab.summary: Fill a datasheet and log three decisions with their approver, then let a peer audit them.

steps.text: Fill the datasheet from the data and the notice
Log three decisions with reason, date and approver
Tag the release with its file fingerprints
Swap with a peer and answer five audit questions
Fix what the peer could not answer

lab.stretch: Add a decision record for the choice of threshold, with the options that were rejected

sessions.title: Scoping with a sponsor
sessions.summary: A vague request becomes an answerable question when the decision, the population, the measure and the success criterion are agreed
outcomes: Ask the questions that turn a request into a decision, a population, a measure and a time frame
Agree success criteria and what is out of scope before any analysis starts
Record the agreement in a scope note the sponsor confirms

lab.title: Scope in six minutes
lab.summary: Turn a vague request into a question in a timed role-play, in threes, and write the scope note.

steps.text: Read the brief and your role card
Round 1: analyst, sponsor, observer
Round 2: rotate the roles
Round 3: rotate the roles
Write your scope note

lab.stretch: Send the scope note as a five-line message and ask the sponsor to confirm one sentence

sessions.title: Pushing back without obstructing
sessions.summary: Saying no is half an answer: name the rule, offer the lawful alternative that serves the same decision, and escalate when it is not yours to decide
outcomes: Refuse an unsafe request by naming the harm and the rule, not by citing policy at the sponsor
Offer a lawful alternative that serves the sponsor's decision
Recognise when to escalate to the data protection officer and record the agreement

lab.title: The risk list
lab.summary: Role-play a request for a risk list and agree a lawful alternative.

steps.text: Read the request and prepare two alternatives
Round 1: analyst, sponsor, observer
Round 2: rotate the roles
Round 3: rotate the roles
Record the agreement and the escalation

lab.stretch: The sponsor insists: write the three-line escalation to the data protection officer

sessions.title: Explaining limits
sessions.summary: A result is finished when its reader knows what it does not show, how sure it is and what it must not be used for
outcomes: State what an analysis cannot show, separately from how uncertain it is
Write a limits statement a non-specialist cannot misread
Choose the capstone engagement and list what its pack must contain

lab.title: Three sentences and the capstone case
lab.summary: Write a three-sentence limits statement and choose the capstone case.

steps.text: Read the result and its interval
List what the analysis cannot show
Write the three-sentence limits statement
Test it against four misreadings
Choose the capstone engagement and open its files

lab.stretch: Rewrite the statement for a student newspaper, without a number that could mislead

days.subtitle: Document the work so others can check it, and hold the three conversations

days.title: Capstone: the responsible-practice pack
days.subtitle: Eight-minute defences: six to present the pack with a short role-play inside, two for the assessor's changed fact

capstone.summary: A responsible-practice pack for one of three synthetic engagements (sharing decision, suppressed tables and log, group comparison, datasheet, analysis log, scope note) in a public repository; eight-minute defence that includes a short role-play
capstone.submission: A public GitHub repository holding the responsible-practice pack for one of the three synthetic engagements: the sharing decision with its conditions, the suppressed tables with the suppression log, the group comparison with intervals and named bias types, the datasheet, the analysis log and the scope note, with a README that links each part and states who approved each release and what the analysis must not be used for. Then an eight-minute defence: six minutes on the pack, including a two-minute role-play with the sponsor, and two minutes in which the assessor changes one fact of the request and the participant revises the sharing decision.
